questions: Do the involuntary eyelid closures affect both eyes at the same time?
Are you fully aware and able to respond normally during these episodes?
Can you voluntarily keep your eyes open when an episode begins?
Are the episodes triggered or worsened by bright light, wind, stress, reading, or watching television?
Do the eyelid spasms improve when you touch your face, rub your eyelids, or use another “trick”?
Do the episodes stop completely when you are asleep?
Do you have eye pain, burning, grittiness, excessive tearing, or marked sensitivity to light?
Do the mouth or facial movements occur independently of the eyelid closures?
Are the eyelid closures consistently worse on one side?
Have you ever had similar involuntary movements elsewhere, such as in your neck, jaw, tongue, or limbs?
Have you taken medicines such as antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, or other dopamine-blocking drugs?
Do you have slowness of movement, stiffness, a resting tremor, or difficulty initiating walking?
Do you ever lose awareness, become confused afterward, or have jerking movements during these episodes?
Did these symptoms begin after an eye injury, eye surgery, or a period of significant eye irritation?
Do the episodes interfere with walking, driving, reading, or other activities because you cannot keep your eyes open?
orders: Direct observation and video recording of a typical episode with bedside testing for distractibility, suggestibility, entrainment, suppressibility, and voluntary eyelid opening
Neuro-ophthalmic examination during and between episodes, including ocular motility, pupils, visual fields, Bell phenomenon, and forced eyelid opening
Prolonged simultaneous video-EEG monitoring, including sleep, to capture a typical episode
Surface electromyography of the orbicularis oculi and frontalis muscles during a typical episode
MRI brain with epilepsy protocol and focused imaging of the brainstem and basal ganglia
Serum anti–acetylcholine receptor and anti-MuSK antibodies
served: acetylcholine receptor, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies
results: 1. Direct observation and video recording of a typical episode with bedside testing for distractibility, suggestibility, entrainment, suppressibility, and voluntary eyelid opening
video-oculography / eye-movement recording: fatigable ptosis with preserved eye movements
2. Neuro-ophthalmic examination during and between episodes, including ocular motility, pupils, visual fields, Bell phenomenon, and forced eyelid opening
ocular motility examination: full in all directions
pupil examination (size, light reaction): equal and reactive
3. Prolonged simultaneous video-EEG monitoring, including sleep, to capture a typical episode
4. Surface electromyography of the orbicularis oculi and frontalis muscles during a typical episode
5. MRI brain with epilepsy protocol and focused imaging of the brainstem and basal ganglia
6. Serum anti–acetylcholine receptor and anti-MuSK antibodies
acetylcholine receptor, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies: elevated acetylcholine receptor antibodies, 16.63 nmol/L
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Seropositive autoimmune ocular myasthenia gravis causing fatigable eyelid ptosis

ALTERNATIVE 1: Bilateral blepharospasm

ALTERNATIVE 2: Focal epileptic eyelid-closure seizures

ALTERNATIVE 3: Functional (psychogenic) eyelid closure disorder
